title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
body_text: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, giving AWS customers access to the fastest open model in its class for persistent agent workloads and rapid task execution. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is engineered for persistent agents and high-throughput enterprise automation across domains including personal assistants, financial document processing, cybersecurity triage, and telecom operations. Built on a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with 30B total parameters and just 3B active per forward pass, it achieves up to 4x the throughput (~410 tokens/sec) and 30% faster task completion over comparable models. Distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra, it handles up to 1M tokens of context via DFlash speculative decoding and integrates directly with popular agent harnesses. The model is fully open-trained on open datasets thereby allowing enterprises to post-train for their own tools, workflows, and policies, and deploy with complete ownership across edge, on-premises, or cloud infrastructure. With SageMaker JumpStart, customers can deploy this model in a few clicks to power their specific AI workloads. To get started with these models, navigate to the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog in the SageMaker console or use the SageMaker Python SDK to deploy the models to your AWS account. For more information about deploying and using foundation models in SageMaker JumpStart, see the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart documentation .

title: 2026 State of Construction Finance Report
summary: Rabbet's 2026 State of Construction Finance Report surveyed commercial real estate developers and construction lenders about costs, contingency, draw cycles, and AI adoption. This is the eighth annual edition. The findings below are drawn directly from that survey.
body_text: 2026 State of Construction Finance: What Real Estate Developers and Construction Lenders Reported Rabbet's 2026 State of Construction Finance Report surveyed commercial real estate developers and construction lenders about costs, contingency, draw cycles, and AI adoption. This is the eighth annual edition. The findings below are drawn directly from that survey. Key findings Construction input costs rose in 2026 while required contingency stayed flat. Developers and lenders report different draw cycle times for the same process. AI is widely trusted for reading documents and rarely trusted for calculations. Most developers holding projects are waiting on capital conditions, not demand. Are construction costs still rising in 2026? Yes. In Rabbet's 2026 State of Construction Finance Report, 75% of developers reported material costs increasing over the past 12 months, 73% reported higher insurance premiums, and 67% reported greater tariff and trade policy impact. Not every input moved. Developers reported permitting timelines, capital availability, and subcontractor stability holding roughly steady over the same period. The 2026 cost pressure is concentrated in materials, insurance, and trade policy rather than in access to capital or labor. How much contingency do construction projects carry in 2026? Most carry between 5% and 10%. In the 2026 State of Construction Finance Report, 84% of both developers and lenders fell in that range. Contingency did not rise to match rising costs. 92% of lenders kept their required baseline contingency unchanged from the prior year, and 58% of developers held their allocations flat. Developers generally carry slightly more contingency than their lenders require. How long does a construction draw take in 2026? It depends on who is measuring. Developers reported a median of 10 days from draw request submission to funding. Lenders reported a median of 6.5 days for the same process. The gap extends to what happens on first review. No developer in the survey reported having a draw request sent back for additional documentation on first review, while 25% of lenders reported sending draw requests back. Asked where a delayed draw package sits, 92% of lenders pointed to the borrower correcting errors or missing documents. No lender identified their own review queue. Developers and lenders are describing the same draw cycle and producing different numbers, because each side is working from its own record of the project. Is AI used in construction finance? Yes, but narrowly. 71% of respondents in the 2026 State of Construction Finance Report trust AI to read and summarize documents. Only 21% trust AI for calculations and quantitative analysis. The trust gap is roughly two to one among developers and roughly eight to one among lenders. No respondent on either side described AI as deeply embedded in their day to day workflow. The most cited barriers to deeper adoption were accuracy and hallucination concerns at 67% and security and data privacy at 58%. ‍ How much time do construction finance teams spend on manual document work? The most common answer on both sides of the loan was 5 to 10 hours per person per week spent handling documents manually. That is close to a full business day each week, per person, spent moving and re-entering information rather than reviewing or deciding. Why are developers putting projects on hold? Capital conditions, not demand. 58% of developers reported having at least some pre-development projects intentionally on hold. Half cited waiting for better funding conditions, while 17% cited demand. A further 33% reported shifting their project mix toward value-add and repositioning. Read the full 2026 State of Construction Finance Report The complete report covers business outlook, capital and pipeline conditions, contingency, draw cycle performance, cost overruns, risk visibility, and AI adoption, with developer and lender results reported separately throughout. Read the 2026 State of Construction Finance Report ‍

title: Local SEO keyword research: A step-by-step guide
summary: Local SEO keyword research in six steps: find the terms customers use, validate intent, and improve visibility on Google Search, Maps, and AI answers.
body_text: Effective local SEO keyword research reveals how nearby customers search for your products or services, from city and neighborhood terms to “near me” queries. AI search has expanded how customers discover and compare local services, so keyword research now needs to account for ranked results and AI-generated answers. In this guide, you’ll learn how to find and prioritize high-intent local keywords, map them to the right pages and profile optimizations, and track their impact on local visibility and conversions. Local search now has two evaluators A search for "best plumber in Denver" now gets judged twice. The first evaluator is the one you know: Google's organic rankings, which match your pages to the query, and the Local Pack, which matches your business profile to it. The second is AI-generated answers: ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity recommending nearby businesses, or an AI Overview composing a response from a handful of cited sources. Both are active discovery surfaces for local customers. But each evaluator assesses a brand differently. Rankings reward how well your pages and profile match the words people search. AI answers weigh the details behind the decision: availability, service area, pricing, licensing, and recurring review themes. Google Business Profile (GBP) data and your website content feed both, but ranking in one and appearing in the other are separate outcomes. One doesn't guarantee the other. So local keyword research now has one list with two jobs: helping your pages rank, and surfacing the questions, service attributes, and location patterns AI systems draw on for answers like "best [service] near [location]." The steps below cover both. What is local SEO keyword research? Local SEO keyword research is the process of finding the search terms people use to discover businesses, products, or services in a specific area. Optimizing your pages for these keywords increases your visibility in organic search results ( SERPs ), which drives more website traffic, inquiries, and sales. Maps visibility and AI-generated answers depend on more than page content, as the sections below explain. Where local keywords appear in Google A search for "[service] in [your location]" can trigger multiple result types at the top of the page, including: Local Services Ads : A row of paid provider cards (often with photos and a "Google Guaranteed" badge) that can appear at the top for service queries, depending on the searcher's location Businesses or Places : A map view with text links listed below, also known as the Google Local Pack . This section might be called "Businesses" or "Places," depending on the type of query used and the searcher's location. Organic results: Local businesses can also appear in the traditional organic results further down the page: Local keywords can trigger both Local Pack and organic search results, but they rank differently. Organic results rely on SEO strategies like on-page optimization and backlinks. Local Pack rankings rely more on GBP optimization, proximity to the searcher, and review signals: the inputs behind what Google calls relevance, distance, and prominence , its three official local ranking factors. Effective keyword research for local SEO identifies which terms trigger the Local Pack, and informs both your website optimization and GBP strategies. Local keyword examples These local keyword examples show how search intent changes by location, urgency, and proximity, so you can choose the right keyword for specific pages and local SEO goals . Keyword type Examples When to use City-level Service plumber boston, dentist austin, roofing contractor denver, family lawyer chicago You serve an entire city or operate multiple locations, and have city-specific service pages. Neighborhood-level plumber south end boston, dentist downtown austin, coffee shop williamsburg brooklyn, yoga studio capitol hill seattle You serve a specific neighborhood, where these terms usually face less competition and reflect more specific local intent. Service + urgency emergency plumber, 24 hour locksmith, same day appliance repair, walk-in clinic You offer emergency or after-hours services. "Near me" plumber near me, coffee shop near me, urgent care near me, pizza delivery near me You're optimizing your Google Business Profile to improve your chances of appearing in the Local Pack. ZIP code + landmark restaurants 10014, dentist near central park, hotels near fenway park, gyms in 78701 Your business is near a landmark, you're targeting specific ZIPs, or you want to capture tourist/visitor searches. Service + attribute wheelchair-accessible dentist, pet-friendly hotel, Spanish-speaking lawyer, family-friendly restaurant Customers use a specific feature, audience need, or service attribute to compare businesses. Commercial or availability modifier affordable plumber boston, dentist open saturday, hotel with free parking, lawyer free consultation Customers compare price, availability, or practical details before choosing a business. Implicit vs. explicit local keywords Explicit local keywords include a location term like "plumber in boston" or "dentist near me ," making the searcher's local intent clear. Implicit local keywords don't specify a location but still trigger local results because the intent is inherently local. A London resident who lost their keys might search "locksmith in london" or "locksmith near me." Both are explicit: the query itself tells Google where to look. "Locksmith london" drops the "in" but still names the city, so it's explicit too, and Google returns near-identical results for both versions. Someone searching just "locksmith" expects nearby options too, but the query never says so. That's an implicit local keyword: Google infers the local intent entirely from the searcher's location. Where results vary most is with the searcher's position. Google resolves every local query against where the searcher is standing, so two people searching from different neighborhoods, or even different postcodes, can see meaningfully different results, especially for implicit queries where location is the only signal Google has. This matters for local SEO because it: Affects ranking eligibility : You can rank for implicit local queries even if your page doesn't use exact "in [city]" phrasing, as long as your GBP optimization, proximity, and review signals are strong. Explains ranking volatility : When rankings change, it's often just Google resolving location intent differently based on user location. Changes how you write copy : You don’t need to say “in London” everywhere on your website. Natural phrasing like “London locksmiths,” “trusted across London,” etc. still creates local relevance. The same logic applies to "near me": repeating the literal phrase in your titles and headers doesn't help you rank for "near me" searches. Google resolves that proximity signal from your Google Business Profile and location data, not from matching those two words on the page. Reinforces the importance of proximity in search : Implicit local searches depend more on distance and prominence, not just keyword matching. That’s why a small local shop can outrank a big brand two miles away. Google uses algorithms to detect local intent and multiple methods to determine a user's location, and delivers local results whether the intent is explicit or implicit. But implicit local keywords let Google decide how local the result should be at the time of the query, not just based on the words used. Because Google decides how local a result should be at query time, treating implicit terms like explicit ones leads you to misdiagnose ranking swings and over-optimize your copy. How to do local keyword research Follow these six steps to perform local keyword research for SEO and AI visibility: List the terms customers use when searching for your solutions in specific locations Find relevant local keywords using research tools Verify local intent in the SERP Analyze competitors to find keyword gaps Map keywords to existing or new pages Research for AI visibility Let's take a closer look at each step. Step 1: List terms for your solutions and locations Before you open any keyword tool, gather the exact words customers use when they contact your business. Call logs, staff notes, and chat transcripts show how real people describe your services, problems, and locations in everyday language. Keyword tools measure demand for phrases people already know to search, but they can't suggest wording they've never seen enough people use. For example, one person may search for "soda," while another looks for "pop": same search intent , different regional wording. A tool has no way of surfacing a variant you didn't already think to enter. Starting with your own customer language catches these variations before you ever open a tool to validate them. Reviews and local community posts (Reddit, Quora, Facebook Marketplace) are worth mining the same way. People describe their needs in the language they'd use in a real conversation. The vocabulary carries across both evaluators, but the query format changes. Someone might type “24-hour plumber South End” into Google and ask ChatGPT, “Can you recommend a 24-hour plumber in South End who can come tonight?” Add both the compact search term and the fuller conversational question to your seed list. List the following types of solution-related terms: General terms for your business type Products and services people are likely to search for Problems or pain points you solve Questions and qualifiers customers use when asking for recommendations Next, list location-related terms at multiple levels of specificity (these make local intent explicit): City Neighborhood ZIP or postcode Landmarks, such as "near Fenway Park," "near downtown," or "near the airport" Step 2: Find relevant local keywords Use keyword research tools to expand your seed list, assess which terms are realistic to rank for, and see which queries surface local business results. If you're starting with a limited budget, Google Keyword Planner is a free local keyword research tool for basic keyword ideas and volume estimates. In the “Discover new keywords” section, enter your seed keywords (from the first step) and location under “Start with keywords.” You can enter a city with Google Keyword Planner, but you can’t use hyper-local areas like neighborhoods or ZIP codes. Click “ Get results .” Google provides broad volume ranges (e.g., "100-1K" instead of exact numbers). For more precise data and local-specific features, use Semrush’s Keyword Magic Tool . Open the tool and enter one of your seed keywords. Add your site’s URL for domain-specific insights, choose your target country, and click “ Search .” You’ll see a list of keywords containing your seed keyword or a variation of it. Use filters to find keywords with local intent. Select “Include keywords ,” choose the “ Any keywords ” option, enter your location modifiers, and click “ Apply .” Review these keywords and select those that match your business and local audience needs. Click the checkboxes next to them, then click “ Send keywords .” Select “Keyword Strategy Builder”, name your list, and click “ Apply .” The keywords you save here can be used in Keyword Strategy Builder in a later step. If you entered your domain name in the Keyword Magic Tool, look at the Personal Keyword Difficulty (“PKD %”) column. That metric indicates the difficulty of ranking your specific website based on your site's authority and content relevance compared to top-ranking competitors. Narrow your list by selecting the “ Personal KD % ” drop-down and setting a custom range of 0-49, which represents terms you have a good chance of ranking for. Then click “ Apply .” Aim for keywords with a good balance of search volume and feasible PKD%. Add relevant keywords to your list by selecting their checkboxes and clicking “ Send keywords .” Next, find implicit keywords. Press the “ X ” on the “Include keywords” filter to remove your location modifiers, and now add those modifiers to the “Exclude keywords” filter to hide explicit keywords. Click “ Apply .” Then, apply a filter to show only queries that trigger the Local Pack. Click “ Advanced filters ,” and from the drop-down below “SERP Features,” select the box next to “ Local pack .” Click “ Apply .” Review these implicit local keywords for search volume and Personal Keyword Difficulty, and send relevant terms to your list. You just filtered this list for the Local Pack. In Step 6, the same filter panel checks it against AI Overviews. Step 3: Verify local intent in the SERP Search the keyword in Google and look at what shows up before you invest time targeting it. Intent type What it means When to target it Typical local SERP output Transactional Ready to hire or buy now Service pages built for quick contact Local Pack, click-to-call Commercial Comparing options before deciding Comparison pages, review-driven content Local Pack (when location-specific) Informational Wants an answer to their query Blog posts, videos, guides, FAQ content AI Overviews, featured snippets, People Also Ask, guides Here's what each of these looks like in an actual search. If someone searches for "emergency plumber near me," they need a plumber now. The "near me" is a proximity signal that implies they want to contact a business. This type of keyword shows transactional intent . Google typically responds to a query like this with a Local Pack. Now, if someone wants to hire a plumber but is comparing options first instead of calling the nearest one, they might search "best plumber in Boston." This type of search signals commercial intent . Google still shows a Local Pack for this query, since the searcher is choosing between businesses. The difference from transactional intent is timing: transactional means ready to take action now, commercial means deciding between businesses. By contrast, if someone is looking for DIY or step-by-step instructions, they would search "how to fix a leaky pipe." This search query indicates informational intent . In this case, the search results would include written content (blogs, landing pages, etc.) and video guides, and increasingly, an AI Overview. If you've published a blog post that directly answers this question, that post has a real chance of being one of the sources the AI Overview cites. Informational queries also open up two more paths to visibility: a featured snippet or a People Also Ask box. Both pull directly from an existing webpage, so if a page on your site clearly answers the question, Google can surface it there, even without a Local Pack. If a keyword's results are only guides, articles, or videos with no Local Pack, treat that as weak local intent. Related read: Learn how to optimize your website for AI Overviews Step 4: Find competitors’ keywords Analyzing competitors' keywords helps you find local search opportunities your business isn't capturing yet. The fastest way to identify your true local competitors is to search a local keyword in Google and see who appears in both the Local Pack and traditional organic results. For example, the below search reveals competing auto shops in Philadelphia. Businesses ranking for your target keywords are your real competitors. They're not just businesses in your category, they're the ones winning the visibility you want. Look at each competitor's business category, shown right under their name. For example, in the above image, Kens Automotive and Boulevard Auto Center are both listed as "Auto repair shop," while Pinnacle Auto Repair and Tires is listed as "Car inspection station." If a competitor uses a relevant category your Google Business Profile doesn't have, add it to your profile and keyword list. That category serves both evaluators: it helps Google judge whether your profile matches a local search, and it gives AI systems a structured label for what your business does. In Step 6, you'll check these labels for gaps across every service you offer. Additionally, check the ratings and review snippets shown under each listing. In the image above, Kens Automotive’s review snippet includes "the prices are fair and the work quality is excellent." For Boulevard Auto Center, it's "great service quality work very convenient." These are customer words. Add any terms that repeat across listings to your keyword list too. You can also use Semrush’s Domain Overview tool to find competitors. Enter your domain, select your country, and click “ Search .” If you have location-specific pages, search those exact URLs (e.g., “site.com/locations/city”). Change “Root Domain” to “ Exact URL ” and click “ Search ” again to find competitors for the location-specific URL you entered. Then, scroll down to “Main Organic Competitors” and note your top competitors’ domains or click “ View details ” to see more. After finding your main competitors, use Semrush’s Keyword Gap tool to find keywords competitors rank for but you don’t. Enter your domain and location, add up to four competitors’ domains and locations, and click “ Compare .” Switch the “Device” to “ Mobile ”, since a lot of local searches happen on mobile devices. Find terms your rivals rank highly for by going to “ Position ” > “ Competitors ” > “ Top 10 .” Exclude competitors’ brand names since you typically don’t want to target them. Go to “ Advanced filters ” and set the fields to “ Exclude ,” “ Keyword ,” and “ Containing .” Put your competitor’s name in the last field, and click “ Apply .” Next, filter for explicit local intent using your location keywords. Go to “ Advanced filters ” and set the fields to “ Include ,” “ Keyword ,” and “ Containing .” Put your location keyword in the last field, and click “ Apply .” Scroll down and look at the “ Untapped ” tab for keywords competitors rank for but you don’t. Review the terms in the table and add relevant keywords to your list. Use the same Volume, KD%, and Intent columns from earlier steps to decide which of these are worth targeting. Step 5: Map your keywords to URLs Now that you have a comprehensive list of terms to target, map each local keyword to a specific page so every important search term is supported by a relevant, optimized URL. The URL you choose is the one you'll optimize to rank, and the content should have a clear, retrievable structure to be cited in an AI-generated result. For multi-location or service-area businesses, keyword mapping often means creating separate pages for city-level keywords (“plumber boston”) and neighborhood-level keywords (“plumber south end boston”). Keyword Strategy Builder can group your keywords into pages automatically, based on relevancy and search intent, to make content planning easier. Open the tool, and under “Keyword lists,” click to open the keyword list you created earlier. Go to the “ Pages ” tab and click “ Create list .” You’ll see your keywords grouped into pages. Each page focuses on a primary keyword. Click the arrow next to a page topic to see: Secondary keywords to target for that page Keyword information like search intent , volume, and keyword difficulty Top-ranking results for inspiration Review the top-ranking results to get inspiration for the type of content you should create. Then, decide which pages you need to create and which pages you need to optimize. If a page doesn’t exist yet, assign it a target URL and create a page that meets the keyword’s search intent. For pages that already exist and need optimization, assign the existing URL. A simple spreadsheet can help you assign URLs. Download our free keyword mapping template , and use it to list all your pages, keywords, and target URLs. Step 6: Research for AI visibility Google's AI generates an AI Overview from a small retrieval set: a handful of pages judged clear and specific enough to answer the query directly. Clear structure, direct answers, and content that pairs your service with your location improve a page's odds of making that set. To find out which of your pages have a shot at this, start with the keyword list you mapped in Step 5. Open Keyword Magic Tool, go to Advanced Filters, select "SERP Features," and check "AI Overview." Click " Apply " to filter your list down to only the keywords that trigger one. Informational, low-difficulty queries, ones with a clear, summarizable answer like a price range, show up here more often than urgent transactional queries, which trigger a Local Pack instead. Open Keyword Overview for one of these keywords and scroll down to SERP Analysis to see exactly which pages made the retrieval set. Six sources are cited here, before the numbered organic rankings even begin. Kwik-Fit appears thrice: twice in the AI Overview's citation list, and again as the #1 organic result with its own backlink and referring-domain data. Click " View SERP " to see what Google generated from that retrieval set. Here's what earned Kwik-Fit's page a spot in that retrieval set. That's a direct, specific answer to the search query (even if it is not the exact amount): what's included, when extra costs apply, and what happens if no adjustment is needed. Structure your own service pages and Google Business Profile descriptions the same way. State the specific answer plainly, and pair your service with your location directly, for example, "Wheel Alignment Services in Philadelphia." Use this same check for entity gaps: service and location combinations your business offers but hasn't clearly labeled anywhere. Go through the pages you mapped in Step 5, and for each one, confirm its primary keyword's exact service and location appears, labeled as such, on your site or GBP. If a competitor's GBP lists "wheel alignment" as a named service (the same category check from Step 4) and yours doesn't, that's an entity gap: an AI system has no label connecting your business to that query, even if you offer the service. To see how your business appears across AI platforms, open Semrush’s AI Visibility Overview and enter your domain. Set the location filter to your target country before reviewing results, since the report defaults to worldwide data. The report shows your mentions and citations across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, plus the specific topics and prompts driving them. Run your top competitors' domains through the same report, and add any relevant prompts where they appear and you don't to your keyword list. This last check ties the workflow together: the customer language you collected in Step 1 became a keyword opportunity in Step 2, was validated in Step 3, expanded in Step 4, assigned to a page in Step 5, and measured here against the pages already earning AI citations. Optimize your Google Business Profile Local keyword research and optimization work best together. Your Google Business Profile (GBP) is a key place to apply your findings because it supports visibility in the Local Pack and Google Maps results. Use relevant local terms naturally in your business description and service names so potential customers can quickly understand what you offer and where you operate. Below is an example of a GBP description : Local keyword research can also help you identify relevant business categories and services. The categories you select can influence local rankings . Only choose categories that reflect your business accurately. Adding non-relevant categories for SEO is against Google’s guidelines . Adding keywords to your GBP content isn’t guaranteed to improve rankings, but using the right terms can help potential customers understand what your business offers and whether it’s right for them. How to handle multiple locations If you have multiple business locations, local keyword research should be done separately for each location to capture differences in search behavior and ranking opportunities. Replacing location names in keywords alone may not uncover all opportunities. Once you have your location-specific keywords, map each relevant keyword cluster to the corresponding location page. For example, the business below targets the specified keyword with one of its location pages. And targets another local keyword on a different location page. Create a separate Google Business Profile for each location too, through your local business listing , to strengthen Local Pack and Maps visibility for that area. How to track your local search visibility Tracking local search visibility helps you measure whether your local SEO efforts are working across Search, Maps, and AI-generated results and spot changes early. Track your Google Search rankings See how your pages perform in local organic results and whether you appear in the Local Pack. Send the keywords you chose in Keyword Strategy Builder to Position Tracking , and monitor your ranking for each one by device and location. Track your Google Maps rankings Understand how your visibility changes across different areas of your target location. Enter the same keywords into Semrush's Map Rank Tracker to visualize rankings on a heatmap, compare performance across specific locations, and see which competitors appear alongside you. Related read: 11 Tips to Improve Your Google Maps SEO Track your AI visibility See whether your business appears in AI-generated answers. Use Semrush's AI Visibility Toolkit to monitor the service, location, and comparison themes from your keyword list across platforms like ChatGPT and Google AI Mode. Improve your local visibility Use local keyword research to turn local demand into visibility, inquiries, and sales. Your next steps: Start with Keyword Magic Tool to build your initial keyword list Prioritize neighborhood-level keywords that match your service area and show favorable competition and conversion potential Map each keyword cluster to the right service page, location page, supporting content, or Google Business Profile field Apply relevant terms naturally across your Google Business Profile categories, services, and business description Create useful location pages with details specific to each genuine business location or service area Track organic rankings with Position Tracking and hyperlocal Maps visibility with Map Rank Tracker Check which target keywords trigger AI Overviews and audit whether your content is easy to retrieve. Use clear service-location pairings, descriptive headings, and direct answers instead of burying key information in dense paragraphs Measure calls, bookings, form submissions, and sales to identify which keywords create business value Consistent implementation across your website and Google Business Profile turns keyword research into local visibility. Start with your highest-priority location or service cluster, measure the results, and expand from there. Local keyword research FAQs Does local SEO still work? Yes, local SEO still works because customers continue to discover nearby businesses through Google Search and Maps, while AI-generated results add another visibility opportunity . Google Maps has more than 2 billion monthly users, and Google reported that AI Overviews reached more than 2 billion monthly users across over 200 countries and territories by July 2025. Local businesses now need visibility across organic results, the Local Pack, Maps, and AI-generated answers. Semrush's AI Overviews study found that over 50% of AI Overviews on desktop and 60% on mobile didn't link to the top organic result. Most often our study saw less than 3 of the URLs from the organic top 10 repeated in the AI Overview. Organic rankings and AI citations are separate outcomes, so track them separately. Can I use ChatGPT for keyword research? Yes, ChatGPT is useful for brainstorming local keyword ideas, generating variations, and clustering topics. However, it doesn’t have a native keyword database or built-in search-volume and difficulty metrics. Use ChatGPT to build your initial seed list and explore subtopics, then validate and prioritize with a dedicated keyword research tool like Semrush’s Keyword Magic Tool, which provides search-volume estimates, keyword difficulty, and SERP feature data. What are the best tools for local keyword research? The best tools for local keyword research combine keyword discovery, location-specific metrics, and competitor insights. Semrush’s Keyword Magic Tool is one of the best tools for local keyword research because it supports large-scale keyword discovery, local filters, and competitive analysis. Other good tools include Semrush’s Keyword Overview, Keyword Gap, and Google’s Keyword Planner. Tool Best For Key Feature Keyword Magic Tool Comprehensive keyword discovery One of the largest databases, local filters, and Keyword Difficulty scoring Keyword Overview Evaluating individual keyword metrics Local search volume, difficulty, intent, SERP features, and SERP analysis for a selected location Keyword Gap Finding competitor keyword opportunities Compare up to five domains to find missing, weak, and untapped keywords Google Keyword Planner Free basic volume estimates Direct Google data but limited local granularity and broad volume ranges How do local keywords affect AI Overview results? Local keywords affect AI Overview results by revealing the service, location, and questions an AI Overview may need to answer. Pages most likely to get cited pair a specific service with a specific location, use structured content instead of dense paragraphs, and back that up with strong local signals like GBP data, consistent NAP information, and reviews. Use Keyword Overview to find which of your local queries trigger an AI Overview, then check the cited sources for these same patterns. Ranking in the top 10 increases your odds of citation, but it isn't a guarantee, content structure and entity clarity matter on their own. Does Google Business Profile optimization help with AI search? Yes, Google Business Profile optimization helps with AI search by giving AI systems a structured, machine-readable source to retrieve directly, unlike a paragraph of website copy an AI has to interpret. Pair your services with your locations in the business description, keep your categories accurate, and maintain consistent NAP information across every listing. These are the same entity signals from Step 6, strengthening them gives AI systems clearer grounds to include your business in a generated answer. Learn more in our Google Business Profile guide . This post was updated in 2026. Excerpts from the original article by Cecilia Meis may remain.

title: Parabolic Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: Cost Reductions Contribute to $3.4M Increase to Net Income from Q1 2026; Company Acquires ConnectAndSell, Expected to Increase FY2026 Revenue to $17M and FY2027 Revenue to $26M Management to Host Second Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call Today, Friday, August 14, 2026 at 4:30 p.m.
body_text: Parabolic Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 14, 2026 PDF Version Cost Reductions Contribute to $3.4M Increase to Net Income from Q1 2026; Company Acquires ConnectAndSell, Expected to Increase FY2026 Revenue to $17M and FY2027 Revenue to $26M Management to Host Second Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call Today, Friday, August 14, 2026 at 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time SEATTLE, Aug. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Banzai International, Inc. (NASDAQ: PARA) (d/b/a “Parabolic” or the “Company”), a leading AI-powered agentic applications technology company, today reported financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 and Subsequent Key Financial & Operational Highlights Company expands vision to Agentic Applications for enterprise with Parabolic rebrand Net Loss for Q2 2026 was $5.0 million, compared to Q1 2026 Net Loss of $8.4 million. The Company achieved net dollar retention in its core customer base of 91% in Q2 2026, an all-time high. Revenue of $2.3 million for Q2 2026, which represented a decrease of $0.4 million from Q1 2026, due to one-time non-recurring revenue in Q1 2026. Gross profit of $1.8 million for Q2 2026, a decrease of $0.4 million compared to Q1 2026. Gross margin was 80.2% for Q2 2026 compared to 80.7% in Q1 2026. Q2 2026 Adjusted EBITDA Loss improved to $1.7 million, compared to an Adjusted EBITDA Loss of $1.9 million in Q1 2026. Reduced net debt by $3.8 million compared to December 31, 2025, bringing net debt to an all-time low. Stockholder’s Equity increased to an all-time high of $12.2 million as of June 30, 2026; converted $7.0 million of debt to equity and raised an additional $8.1 million of equity since December 31, 2025. Customer base includes over 150,000 total customers who have purchased or subscribed to Parabolic products. Closed the acquisition of the assets of ConnectAndSell, expected to increase annual revenue and expand AI Platform capabilities beginning in third quarter 2026. “Our proposed name change to Parabolic represents more than a new brand. This change reflects where we believe the future of software is headed, and the path to strategic growth through investment in high potential businesses. Our continued aim is to build a business that delivers profitable growth both organically and strategically. For example, the recently announced acquisition of ConnectAndSell, an AI sales acceleration platform, will begin contributing to company results in the third quarter of this year and will transform the scale of our business in 2H 2026 and FY 2027 when we estimate 2027 revenue growth of 50% year-over-year. “ConnectAndSell serves approximately 250 B2B organizations such as Intuit, RingCentral, Truckstop, and SAP across financial services, healthcare, technology, and other industries. ConnectAndSell’s FY 2025 revenue was $14.7 million, with a gross margin of 86%, and an average revenue per customer of approximately $59,000. “I am pleased to report the second quarter operating losses have decreased primarily from executing on the cost management plan that we announced in May. Additionally, I am pleased that Parabolic's management is making further cost reductions, which we expect will meaningfully reduce operating expenses within this calendar year. “Overall, our revenue trend was influenced by one-time non-recurring revenue recognized in Q1 2026. We saw many bright spots including all-time high NRR in and growing bookings in our enterprise segment, consistently high gross margin, and meaningful decreases in operating expenses as a result of the management actions announced in May. Additionally, we are seeing improvements in leading indicators within the sales pipeline and strong customer retention statistics,” said Joe Davy, Founder and CEO of Parabolic. “During the quarter, we strengthened our balance sheet by retiring debt totaling $4.5 million through cash payments and share conversions and improving Stockholder’s Equity by $4.1 million. “Looking ahead, we have announced a rebranding and have aligned our business units to align leadership and go-to-market execution with our evolved vision. The Company’s operations are now organized into three business units: ConnectAndSell, the Company’s AI sales acceleration platform, Banzai, our enterprise video business, and CreateStudio, our AI-powered video content creation platform. These business units are supported by a cost-efficient shared service function. “We also maintain an active pipeline of potential acquisition opportunities across key industries where we have strong sector experience and can leverage our AI platform and experience to add value and strategic operational acceleration. The recent acquisition of ConnectAndSell is a demonstration of a successful execution of our strategic growth goal,” concluded Davy. title: ‘These aren’t strangers’: Protecting the community they call home
summary: Helping Florida firefighters stay connected when every second counts
body_text: Helping Florida firefighters stay connected when every second counts August 18, 2026 As Hurricane Idalia approached northern Florida in 2023, a call came in that Live Oak firefighters won’t forget. A large oak tree had crashed through a home, trapping a man in his bed. The force of the impact pushed the roof down onto him and drove the bed through the floor. Working alongside neighboring agencies, crews quickly coordinated resources, lifted the tree and safely rescued the resident. “The amount of crews pulling together to get this done was a phenomenal feat,” recalls Kyle Nickerson, Assistant Fire Chief with the Live Oak Fire Department. For the firefighters serving the City of Live Oak, moments like these highlight the importance of teamwork and communication. Located between Jacksonville and Tallahassee, the department operates from a single station with 14 personnel serving roughly 8,500 residents. Last year alone, firefighters responded to nearly 1,900 calls for service, including structure, vehicle and brush fires, medical emergencies, vehicle collisions, gas leaks, hazardous conditions and severe weather incidents. Firefighters with the Live Oak Fire Department responded to nearly 1,900 calls in 2025, including structure, vehicle, and brush fires, medical emergencies, vehicle collisions and gas leaks. The rescue during Hurricane Idalia also reinforced how critical clear communication can be during an emergency. As crews coordinated resources and responded to changing conditions, information needed to be shared quickly and accurately. Through a grant from Enbridge’s Safe Community First Responder Program, the department added new communication technology to its fire apparatus, helping firefighters hear radio traffic more clearly and communicate with one another while responding to emergencies. “It’s actually a complete game changer for us,” says Will Johnson, senior firefighter with the Live Oak Fire Department. “Before, we were always asking each other, ‘What was said over the radio?’ With the engine noise of the fire truck, along with the sirens, it makes it really hard to hear.” You may also like: Safe Community First Responder Program Enriching lives across North America: Mapping our community investment strategy Enbridge’s economic impact on Florida For a small department, investments in equipment that improve firefighter safety and effectiveness can have a meaningful impact. Support from organizations like Enbridge helps the Live Oak Fire Department acquire tools that can be difficult to fund through its operational budget. Safe Community grants dating back to 2023 have supported the department’s equipment needs by funding portable radios, emergency box lights and thermal imaging cameras. The department hopes future purchases will include additional Firecom radio headset systems and a battery-powered cut-off saw for motor vehicle collisions and other emergencies. “We’re super grateful and thankful to have something like this available to us,” says Johnson. For many members of the department, serving the community is personal. Their families live in Live Oak, their children attend local schools and the people they help are often neighbors and friends. “Nobody's going to do this better than we will because this is where we're from," says Nickerson. "These aren't strangers.” That connection is what drives the department every day. “When I see them later on, I can look them in the eye and say, ‘We brought forth every bit of effort we possibly could,’ ” remarks Nickerson. “This is our home. We want our home to do well.” You may also like: Safety ‘Working together benefits everyone’: Safety starts with collective training Community Volunteer EMTs get a new ride to the rescue Safety Standing shoulder to shoulder with volunteer rescue crews

title: How do perimenopause and menopause affect weight?
summary: Weight gain may continue through the menopause transition, and it can happen even when you lead an active lifestyle and focus on healthy eating.
body_text: How do perimenopause and menopause affect weight? Written by the Progyny Editorial Team. Reviewed by the Progyny Clinical Team — July 2026. Many women notice weight gain that starts before obvious signs of perimenopause.* Weight gain may continue through the menopause transition, and it can happen even when you lead an active lifestyle and focus on healthy eating. (*We’ll use the term peri/menopause in this article to refer to perimenopause and menopause together. We use “women” to acknowledge anyone who goes through peri/menopause.) Weight fluctuation is often natural and there are a range of healthy body types. For some people, however, weight gain during this time may be frustrating or raise health concerns. Managing weight in midlife can help you stay on a path to healthy aging and may boost energy and mood. Let’s talk more about this, keeping in mind that everyone is different. What causes weight gain during midlife? For many of us, midlife weight gain happens because our metabolism slows. One factor is that beginning around age 30, we start to lose muscle – and muscle burns more calories than fat. Weight gain may also happen because when estrogen declines during perimenopause, our bodies don’t handle sugars as well as they once did. Our lifestyle also affects our weight: Midlife can be a time of stress. Stress influences our nutrition, ability to exercise, quality of sleep, and energy to make healthy changes. Poor sleep is linked with weight gain. There are many reasons we may not sleep well (including peri/menopause itself). We may not always eat nutritious, balanced meals, and our physical activity level might be less than it used to be. Of course, family history and genetics play a role in our body type and how our bodies change. Health conditions and medicines may lead to weight changes, as well. Where does peri/menopause fit in? Peri/menopause isn’t usually the main driver of weight gain, but it may be a factor. Hormone changes from menopause may affect where we store fat. It often shifts from our bottoms and thighs to our lower belly (abdomen). This type of abdominal fat may raise health risks. In addition, peri/menopause may cause symptoms that contribute to weight gain. For example, anxiety and night sweats can disturb sleep and add to stress, making it hard to manage weight. Does menopause hormone therapy (MHT) help? MHT doesn’t directly affect weight, and it’s not prescribed for weight loss. However, it may help improve disrupted sleep. MHT may also help reduce fat storage in the belly, although more research is needed. Not everyone can take MHT. If it’s not right for you, there are non-hormonal medicines and strategies to help manage symptoms affecting sleep. Strategies and support for a healthy weight Weight management is about finding the path that works for you, not anyone else. (It’s not about what anyone else thinks, either.) All women’s bodies change over our lifetime, and that is OK and natural. Work with your healthcare provider to track your health and feel good about yourself. And if you want to make small changes, think about what matters most to you. How does a healthy weight connect with that? Identifying this motivation is essential. Take care of YOU first Taking care of your overall well-being is an important part of managing weight. Are you sleeping well and practicing self-care? That can often be a good place to start. Allow yourself time for the things that ground you. Ideas include: Relaxation techniques like deep breathing or meditation Social connection in a group or volunteer setting Nights out with your partner or a friend Time alone with your thoughts or a good book Doing a hobby you love Healthy eating in midlife Continue balanced eating. Emphasize lean protein, fruits, vegetables, dairy, healthy fats, and whole grains. Protein is more important as we age since it helps preserve muscle. ( Calculate your protein needs here .) Consume fewer calories in your 40s and 50s. Your daily calorie needs go down as metabolism slows. One direct way to do this is to limit empty calories from sugar, processed foods, and alcohol. Ask for support. A registered dietitian can optimize your nutrition and personalize strategies for you. And look for support at home so you can plan, prepare, and eat healthy together. Physical activity that’s right for you Do what you enjoy. Aim to get your heart pumping 30 minutes, 5 days a week. You can do this in smaller chunks that add up. The best types of activity: the ones you enjoy! A friend, class, or trainer can all help you get motivated. Focus on strength. Strengthening helps you maintain muscle, manage weight, and preserve bone health. It makes daily activities easier, too. Try working up to at least 2 days of strength training a week. Work together with your provider Your provider can provide personalized guidance and referrals if needed. They can also determine if medicine (such as GLP-1s) may support you. A menopause provider has specialized expertise for this phase of life. Your Progyny Care Advocate can help you find in-network nutritionists and menopause specialists. We can also provide education, coaching, and support as you make lifestyle changes. Disclaimer: The information provided by Progyny is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare provider for medical guidance.

title: The Biggest Mistake Organizations Make About Digital Sovereignty
summary: Digital sovereignty is now a business resilience issue, not just a compliance requirement. Learn why data location alone isn't enough and how organizations can reduce risk from legal, operational, and geopolitical dependencies.
body_text: A few years ago, digital sovereignty was largely viewed as a compliance conversation. If you stored data in the right geography, met the right regulatory requirements, and satisfied a handful of audit questions, you could generally move on. That’s no longer the case. Today, sovereignty has become a board-level discussion. Governments are rewriting policies. Regulators are increasing scrutiny. And business leaders are starting to recognize that sovereignty isn’t just about where data resides – it’s about how organizations continue operating when geopolitical, legal, or operational assumptions suddenly change. In the first episode of our STRIVE series on digital sovereignty, I sat down with Max Mortillaro, co-founder and Chief Research Officer at Osmium Data Group. Together, we unpack what sovereignty actually means, why the conversation has accelerated so quickly, and where organizations are most likely to get it wrong. Watch the full episode. Key Takeaways Digital sovereignty is no longer just a compliance issue – it has become a resilience and business continuity concern. Data location is only one piece of the puzzle. Jurisdiction, operations, technology dependencies, and governance all matter. Many organizations focus on technical controls before understanding the business problem they’re trying to solve. Geopolitical uncertainty is accelerating sovereignty initiatives, particularly across Europe. There is no such thing as a perfectly sovereign environment. Every organization must make informed trade-offs between risk, cost, and operational requirements. Why Data Location Isn’t the Whole Story One of the most common misconceptions around digital sovereignty is that it begins and ends with geography. If data is stored in a local data center, the thinking goes, the sovereignty problem has been solved. It’s an understandable assumption. After all, many of the early conversations around sovereignty focused heavily on data residency requirements and where information could legally be stored. But as Max points out during our discussion, that’s only one dimension of a much larger challenge. Sovereignty isn’t simply about where a data center sits. It’s also about who operates it, which laws apply to it, who has access to it, and what dependencies exist behind the scenes. A cloud service may be physically located within a specific country, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s insulated from legal, operational, or technological influence originating elsewhere. That’s where the conversation becomes significantly more complex. The Hidden Dependencies Most Organizations Overlook When organizations first begin exploring sovereignty, they often approach it as a technology project. They evaluate hosting locations. They assess replication strategies. They examine where workloads should run. Those conversations are important, but they can also create a false sense of confidence. As Max explains, modern technology environments are built on layers of dependencies that aren’t always visible. A service may appear local on the surface but it may be relying on infrastructure, management systems, telemetry services, or operational controls that exist elsewhere. That’s why sovereignty isn’t simply a question of location. It’s a question of influence. Who ultimately controls the service? Which legal jurisdiction applies when disputes arise? What happens if geopolitical tensions introduce new restrictions, regulations, or limitations on access? These aren’t hypothetical questions anymore. They’re becoming part of real-world risk assessments. Sneak Peek: Sovereignty Is More Than a Technical Problem In this segment from the conversation, Max explains why organizations often start sovereignty discussions in the wrong place – and why understanding the legal, operational, and business objectives must come before any technology decisions. Why Europe Is Driving the Conversation One of the most interesting parts of our discussion focuses on why sovereignty has become such a dominant topic across Europe. The answer isn’t just regulation; it’s dependency. European organizations have become increasingly aware that many of the technologies they rely on every day are owned, operated, or governed outside of their direct control. For years, that reality was largely accepted as part of the global technology ecosystem. Today, that assumption is being reevaluated. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations, and increasing concern around strategic autonomy have pushed sovereignty higher on the priority list for governments and enterprises alike. What was once considered an edge case has become a mainstream business concern. The result is a growing recognition that resilience isn’t only about recovering from technical failures. It’s also about understanding and managing external dependencies before they become business disruptions. Sovereignty and Resilience Are the Same Conversation One of the themes that you’ll see repeatedly surfacing throughout the discussion is how closely sovereignty and resilience are connected. At first glance, they may seem like separate disciplines. One focuses on governance, regulation, and control. The other focuses on recovery, continuity, and operational readiness. In practice, they’re deeply intertwined. If a business cannot access critical systems because of a geopolitical event, regulatory restriction, or third-party dependency, the outcome isn’t very different from other disruptions organizations spend years preparing for. The business still needs to operate. Customers still need to be served. Recovery still needs to happen. That’s why I increasingly view sovereignty through the same lens as cyber resilience. Both are fundamentally about reducing exposure to events that could disrupt operations and preparing the organization to continue functioning when those events occur. Start With the Business Problem Perhaps the most practical advice Max shares is also the simplest. Before evaluating sovereign cloud offerings, before engaging vendors, and before debating technical architectures, organizations should first understand what problem they’re trying to solve. That means understanding: Which business processes are most critical. Which data assets matter most. Which regulatory requirements apply. Which risks are truly being mitigated. Only after those questions are answered does it make sense to evaluate technology options. Too often, organizations start with solutions and work backward toward the problem. Sovereignty requires the opposite approach. The strategy should come first. The architecture follows. Why There Is No Perfect Answer One of the realities leaders need to accept is that there is no such thing as a perfectly sovereign environment. Every organization operates within a network of dependencies. Every technology choice introduces trade-offs. Every risk decision involves balancing operational requirements, compliance obligations, cost considerations, and business outcomes. The goal isn’t perfection. The goal is understanding those trade-offs well enough to make informed decisions. Organizations that approach sovereignty as a binary yes-or-no question often find themselves frustrated. Organizations that approach it as a risk-management exercise tend to make better progress. Why This Conversation Matters Digital sovereignty is moving quickly from a niche compliance topic to a strategic business issue. Boards are asking questions. Regulators are increasing scrutiny. Customers are becoming more aware of where their data lives and who controls it. At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty continues to reshape how organizations think about risk. That doesn’t mean every company needs a radical sovereignty transformation tomorrow. But it does mean that the organizations that start building a clear strategy today will be in a much stronger position than those who wait until the conversation becomes unavoidable. Sovereignty isn’t a technology decision masquerading as a business problem. It’s a business problem that requires legal, operational, and technical decisions working together. Watch the Full Episode In this installment, Max and I explore: What digital sovereignty actually means. Why data location alone isn’t enough. The legal and operational dimensions organizations often overlook. How geopolitical developments are influencing sovereignty strategies. Why sovereignty and resilience are becoming inseparable. Watch now. FAQs Q: What is digital sovereignty? A: Digital sovereignty refers to an organization’s ability to maintain control over its data, technology, operations, and governance within specific legal and jurisdictional boundaries. Q: Is digital sovereignty the same as data residency? A: No. Data residency is one component of sovereignty, but sovereignty also includes legal jurisdiction, operational control, technology dependencies, and governance. Q: Why has digital sovereignty become more important recently? A: Growing geopolitical uncertainty, evolving regulations, and increasing concern about technology dependencies have accelerated interest in sovereignty initiatives. Q: What is the biggest mistake organizations make? A: Treating sovereignty as a purely technical challenge instead of a broader business risk and resilience issue. Q: How does sovereignty relate to cyber resilience? A: Both disciplines focus on maintaining operational continuity in the face of disruptions, whether those disruptions are technical, legal, geopolitical, or regulatory. Q: Where should organizations begin? A: Start by understanding the business outcomes you’re trying to protect, the risks you’re trying to mitigate, and the data and processes that are most critical to your operations. Alex Zinin is VP/GM of Managed Service Providers at Commvault.

title: 6 Best Voice Dictation Tools for Students | Willow August 2026
summary: We ranked the 6 best voice dictation tools for university students in August 2026 by accuracy, latency, vocabulary learning, and value for a student budget.
body_text: Student writing doesn't slow down, and your dictation tool shouldn't either. The gap between speaking at 150 words per minute and typing at 40 adds up fast, but only if the tool keeps up without leaving you correcting every other sentence. That same constraint applies whether you're working on a Windows lab computer, a Mac laptop, or switching between the two mid-semester. We ranked the best voice dictation tools for universities and students on the factors that actually matter: accuracy on discipline-specific vocabulary, latency you won't feel, coverage across Mac, Windows, and iOS environments, and pricing that fits a student budget. TLDR: Speaking runs at 150 WPM vs. 40 WPM typing, so dictation can close a real output gap across a heavy assignment load. Latency separates the field more than any other spec: most tools run 500ms to 1 second, which is long enough to break concentration mid-sentence. Tools without learnable dictionaries can struggle with field-specific terms, quietly eroding the time savings that made voice input appealing. Dragon Professional requires 20 to 30 minutes of voice training upfront and doesn't travel well across devices, which limits it for most students. The top-ranked tool in this list runs at ~200ms latency with 98%+ accuracy and an Auto-Dictionary that picks up course-specific terminology across Mac, Windows, and iOS without per-device setup. University IT teams and research programs can deploy it org-wide with shared custom dictionaries, admin controls, SOC 2 Type II certification, and HIPAA compliance built in from day one. What Is Voice Dictation for Students? Students write constantly. Essays, discussion posts, lab reports, study notes, and the occasional AI prompt stretched across a deadline-heavy week. Voice dictation tools convert spoken words into text using AI-powered speech recognition, letting you produce written content by talking instead of typing. Most people speak at around 150 words per minute but type closer to 40, a gap confirmed by student typing speed data from a 1,301-person university cohort. Across an assignment-heavy semester, that output gap adds up. A 2025 piece in Nature on voice dictation in academic writing found similar patterns among researchers and graduate students, noting that AI-powered dictation tools reduce both output friction and physical strain over time. For more on voice dictation insights , the research keeps pointing the same direction. For students juggling lectures, reading, and writing all at once, voice dictation offers a way to keep pace with the volume without slowing down every time words need to reach a page. Best Overall Voice Dictation Tool for Students: Willow Voice Willow Voice is built for the student workflow: ~200ms latency means text lands almost the instant you finish a sentence, so the next thought doesn't evaporate while you wait. Built-in tools like Apple's voice dictation run at 700ms or more, long enough to break concentration mid-sentence. Willow activates with a single keypress (fn on Mac or Alt+Space on Windows) and works in any application without switching windows or tabs. Accuracy holds up where it matters most. Willow reaches 98%+ accuracy and produces 3x fewer errors than built-in dictation tools , which means the correction overhead that typically erodes speed gains stays small enough to make dictation a genuine net win. For context, a peer-reviewed evaluation of AI-based speech recognition found word error rates ranging from under 1% in controlled settings to over 50% in complex or multi-speaker scenarios, a range that shows exactly why accuracy on domain-specific vocabulary matters. Personalization That Builds Over Time The gap between a general-purpose dictation tool and one that actually fits your workflow is vocabulary. Willow's Auto-Dictionary picks up course-specific terms, proper nouns, citation formats, and field-specific language without manual setup. Custom vocabulary overrides are available for both personal and shared dictionaries when a professor's name or a technical term keeps transcribing incorrectly. For university programs and research groups deploying Willow across a department, shared dictionaries let an administrator push terminology updates to every member at once, with no individual reconfiguration needed. Beyond Transcription Willow Scribe , activated with Fn + Control on Mac and Alt+Shift+Space on Windows, goes further than word-for-word capture. It generates complete written content from voice prompts, which means you can speak a rough idea and get a structured draft back, or ask it to rewrite a selected passage without touching the keyboard. For students working across Mac, Windows, and iOS, vocabulary and settings carry over across devices without per-device setup. You can speak notes on a Windows desktop in the computer lab, switch to a Mac laptop at home, and pick up on your phone between classes, all from the same configuration with no re-setup required. For university IT teams managing mixed-device environments, that cross-device continuity removes the per-user configuration overhead that makes most dictation tools impractical to roll out across a department or program. Privacy is built on enterprise-grade infrastructure: Willow is SOC 2 Type II certified and HIPAA compliant with zero data retention, so the notes and drafts you're capturing by voice aren't stored after the session ends. For research programs with FERPA or IRB data handling requirements, that architecture means voice audio is processed and discarded by default, removing it from the compliance question without any additional configuration. Typeless Typeless is built for students who want a clean, distraction-free dictation experience, focused on getting spoken words onto the page accurately and quickly. It works across browsers and major operating systems, and the interface stays out of your way while you speak. There's no steep learning curve and no subscription gate blocking core features, which gives students a low-friction entry point for basic voice-to-text. The limitation is vocabulary depth. Custom vocabulary support is limited, which means discipline-specific terminology in fields like biochemistry, law, or economics may require more correction passes than tools with learnable dictionaries. For students producing field-specific content regularly, that correction overhead can quietly cancel out the time saved by speaking. VoiceInk VoiceInk is a Mac-only voice dictation app built around on-device processing using Apple Silicon. Your audio never leaves your device, which appeals to students with privacy concerns about cloud-based transcription. Offline transcription is fully functional, no subscription is required after purchase, and the interface is clean for basic tasks. The Mac-only constraint is the main limit. Students who move between a Windows lab and a MacBook, or who need voice input on their phone between classes, will find VoiceInk's single-device scope frustrating. There is no iOS app and no cross-device vocabulary sync. Latency also runs higher than cloud-based tools during longer sessions, so extended essay drafts can feel slower than alternatives. Monologue Monologue is an AI-powered voice dictation app designed around the student workflow, with features tuned for essays, research notes, and lecture capture. The app runs on iOS and Mac, covering most devices students actually use. Accuracy is solid for general academic vocabulary, and the interface is clean with a low learning curve, so it stays out of your way while you write. Custom vocabulary depth is limited compared to tools built for domain-heavy fields, and there's no Windows support, which matters on campuses where lab computers run Windows. Collaborative features are absent, so university IT departments looking to deploy across departments will find it a poor fit. For an individual student on a Mac or iPhone, Monologue is a reasonable pick. Dragon Professional Dragon Professional is one of the most recognized names in voice dictation, with decades of use across legal, medical, and academic settings. In university settings, it has historically been the go-to choice for accessibility offices and institutional IT teams supporting students with disabilities. Its Windows-only architecture fits well in Windows-heavy campus environments but creates a gap for students and faculty who move between Windows lab computers and Mac laptops throughout the day. The tool works as a desktop application that runs locally on Windows, meaning audio never touches a cloud server. That architecture appeals to institutions with strict data policies, though it also means the software carries a steeper hardware requirement than browser-based alternatives. Aqua Voice Aqua Voice is a voice dictation tool built around a conversational interaction model. You can issue commands in plain language, like "delete that last sentence" or "make this more formal," and the tool responds, reducing the need to switch back to manual editing. It supports Mac and Windows but lacks iOS support and offline mode. Pricing sits at around $8/month, making it one of the more affordable options here. For university programs and research groups, Willow is SOC 2 Type II certified and HIPAA compliant with zero data retention, removing voice audio from the compliance question for FERPA-sensitive workflows and IRB research protocols by default. Administrators can push shared custom dictionaries with course-specific terminology to every member at once through a single admin view, making org-wide rollout viable without per-user reconfiguration. FAQs How do I choose the right voice dictation tool from this list? Start with your platform and budget: VoiceInk is Mac-only, Monologue covers Mac and iOS, and Dragon runs on Windows. If you move between a Windows desktop and a Mac or need mobile access on iOS, only Willow Voice covers all three without per-device reconfiguration. From there, consider whether you need vocabulary learning, offline capability, or a free tier to test before committing. For teams and university programs deploying across a department, Willow Voice also offers shared dictionaries and admin controls that the other tools here don't support. Which voice dictation tool works best for students with highly technical or discipline-specific vocabulary? Tools with automatic vocabulary learning handle academic terminology far better than static alternatives. A peer-reviewed scoping review on speech-to-text for student writing found that writing performance gains are most consistent when tools handle domain-specific vocabulary accurately, not by relying on static general-purpose models. Willow Voice picks up course-specific terms, professor names, and field-specific language without manual setup, and that vocabulary carries across Mac, Windows, and iOS so you don't repeat the process on each device. Dragon Professional also learns vocabulary but requires 20 to 30 minutes of voice training before personalization kicks in, and it runs on Windows only, which limits it if your workflow spans multiple platforms. What is the difference between transcription tools and AI-assisted dictation tools? Transcription tools convert speech to text word-for-word, leaving all editing and structuring to you. AI-assisted tools like Willow Voice go further by generating complete drafts from voice prompts, removing filler words, and formatting output automatically, so the gap between speaking and a usable first draft shrinks considerably. For professional and enterprise workflows where output quality matters alongside speed, that distinction affects how much post-processing time each session actually costs. Final Thoughts on Voice Dictation Tools for University Students The best voice dictation tools for universities and students earn that label by keeping the correction loop small. title: Renouvelables en Europe : TotalEnergies acquiert les activités renouvelables de Shell et cède 50 % d’un portefeuille d’actifs développés à KKR
summary: Paris, le 3 août 2026 – En ligne avec sa stratégie Integrated Power en Europe visant à se concentrer sur certains marchés dérégulés, telle qu’illustrée par la transaction récente avec EPH, et avec son modèle d’affaires d’optimisation de l’allocation de capital dans les énergies renouvelables, TotalEnergies annonce la signature de deux transactions en Europe : […]
body_text: Paris, le 3 août 2026 – En ligne avec sa stratégie Integrated Power en Europe visant à se concentrer sur certains marchés dérégulés, telle qu'illustrée par la transaction récente avec EPH , et avec son modèle d'affaires d'optimisation de l'allocation de capital dans les énergies renouvelables, TotalEnergies annonce la signature de deux transactions en Europe : L'acquisition d'un portefeuille renouvelable de 4 GW auprès de Shell, dont 500 MW d'actifs solaires et éoliens en opération ou en construction. TotalEnergies a signé un accord avec Shell pour l'acquisition de l'ensemble de ses activités renouvelables terrestres en Europe, incluant 500 MW d'actifs solaires et éoliens en opération ou en construction principalement situés en Italie et aux Pays-Bas et 3,5 GW de pipeline de projets solaires, éoliens et de stockage par batterie en Italie, au Royaume-Uni et en Espagne. Ce portefeuille d'actifs sera détenu à 100 % par TotalEnergies à l'issue de la transaction dont la finalisation, prévue d'ici la fin 2026, reste soumise à l'approbation des autorités compétentes. Cette transaction vient compléter les activités de production d'électricité de TotalEnergies dans ces quatre marchés clés pour le déploiement de sa stratégie Integrated Power en Europe, notamment son portefeuille d'actifs renouvelables en Europe qui s'élève à près de 10 GW de capacités brutes installées ou en construction et 27 GW en développement. La cession à KKR de 50 % d'un portefeuille de 1,2 GW d'actifs renouvelables déjà largement développés, pour une valeur d'entreprise de 1,8 milliard d'euros. Confirmant sa capacité à exécuter année après année les cessions partielles conformément à son modèle d'affaires dans les renouvelables, TotalEnergies a signé un accord avec un fonds d'assurance géré par KKR, société d'investissement de premier plan, pour la vente de 50 % d'un portefeuille d'actifs solaires et éoliens terrestres de 1,2 GW en Europe. La valeur d'entreprise du portefeuille s'élève à 1,8 milliard d'euros. La transaction porte sur un portefeuille d'actifs en Allemagne, Espagne, France et Pologne. L'électricité produite par ces actifs est déjà vendue à des tiers ou sera commercialisée par TotalEnergies. TotalEnergies conservera une participation de 50 % dans ces actifs qu'elle continuera d'opérer après la finalisation de la transaction, prévue en 2026 et soumise aux conditions habituelles. « Conformément à notre stratégie, ces deux transactions nous permettent d'optimiser notre allocation de capital dans les énergies renouvelables et de poursuivre la mise en œuvre de la stratégie Integrated Power. L'acquisition des actifs renouvelables terrestres de Shell en Europe nous permet de conforter nos positions de production d'électricité dans certains marchés clés dérégulés en Europe et de poursuivre la mise en œuvre de notre stratégie intégrée sur la chaîne de valeur de l'électricité en complétant la production flexible des centrales électriques à gaz de TTEP, notre coentreprise avec EPH, notamment en Italie, aux Pays-Bas et au Royaume-Uni », a déclaré Stéphane Michel, Directeur général Gas, Renewables & Power chez TotalEnergies . « Par ailleurs, avec cet accord avec KKR, nous démontrons une nouvelle fois notre capacité à mettre en œuvre notre business model dans les énergies renouvelables pour qu'Integrated Power atteigne un ROACE de 12 % à horizon 2030 ».
